cor.heading: Cost of Goods Sold (“COGS”)
cor.text: COGS was $1,534 million (62 percent of net sales) and $1,644 million (63 percent of net sales) for the three months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, respectively, and $6,624 million (48 percent of net sales) and $6,918 million (51 percent of net sales) for the nine months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, respectively. The change in the three months ended September 30, 2026 was primarily driven by lower volumes, lower input costs, and ongoing cost and productivity action s. The change in the nine months ended September 30, 2026 was driven by lower volumes, lower input costs, ongoing cost and productivity actions, and net royalty improvement partially offset by unfavorable currency impacts .

costs.text: Proceeds of loans under the Vylor Delayed Draw Term Facility were intended to be used to finance the Vylor Separation and to pay fees, costs and expenses related thereto. The maturity date of the Vylor Delayed Draw Term Facility was approximately one year from its closing date. Amounts borrowed under the Vylor Delayed Draw Term Facility were subject to an interest rate per annum equal to Term SOFR plus the applicable margin. There were no borrowings outstanding under the Vylor Delayed Draw Term Facility, and the facility was terminated on October 1, 2026.

rd.heading: Research and Development Expense (“R&D”)
rd.text: R&D expense was $397 million (16 percent of net sales) and $351 million (13 percent of net sales) for the three months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, respectively, and $1,126 million (8 percent of net sales) and $1,061 million (8 percent of net sales) for the nine months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, respectively. The increase in R&D expense is in support of the company’s long-term investment plans and was primarily driven by increases in salaries, contract labor, outside contract

sga.heading: Selling, General and Administrative Expenses (“SG&A”)
sga.text:
SG&A expenses were $732 million (30 percent of net sales) and $725 million (28 percent of net sales) for the three months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, respectively. The change was primarily driven by increases in personnel and information technology costs and legal support fees, partially offset by lower bad debt expense, promotion and advertising fees, consulting and professional fees and commissions.

SG&A expenses were $2,773 million (20 percent of net sales) and $2,632 million (20 percent of net sales) for the nine months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, respectively. The change was primarily driven by unfavorable currency impacts and increases in personnel and information technology costs, legal support fees, and consulting and professional fees, partially offset by lower promotion and advertising fees and commissions.

nonop.heading: Interest Expense
nonop.text: Interest expense was $75 million and $46 million for the three months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, respectively, and $158 million and $134 million for the nine months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, respectively. The increases were driven by higher commercial paper outstanding, higher refinancing rate of the May 2026 senior notes, and cost of new credit facilities.

tax.text: The company’s provision for income taxes on continuing operations was $479 million for the nine months ended September 30, 2026 on pre-tax income from continuing operations of $1,894 million, resulting in an effective tax rate of 25.3 percent. The effective tax rate was unfavorably impacted by a $45 million charge associated with various transactions executed to facilitate the planned separation of its businesses, a $50 million charge associated with the Discretionary Pension Contribution, valuation allowances on certain foreign tax credits, and withholding taxes on repatriation of cash held outside of the U.S. primarily from current year earnings. Those unfavorable impacts were partially offset by $49 million of net tax benefits associated with changes in deferred taxes and accruals for certain prior year tax positions, as well as $31 million of net tax benefits related to intellectual property realignment.

Corteva considers the borrowing costs and lending terms when selecting the source to fund its operations and working capital needs.

da.text: Operating EBITDA is defined as earnings (loss) (i.e., income (loss) from continuing operations before income taxes) before interest, depreciation, amortization, non-operating benefits (costs), foreign exchange gains (losses), and net unrealized gain or loss from mark-to-market activity for certain foreign currency derivative instruments that do not qualify for hedge accounting, excluding the impact of significant items and separation costs. Non-operating benefits (costs) consists of non-operating pension and OPEB credits (costs), tax indemnification adjustments and environmental remediation and legal costs associated with legacy businesses and sites. Tax indemnification adjustments relate to changes in indemnification balances, as a result of the application of the terms of the Tax Matters Agreement, between Corteva and Dow and/or DuPont that are recorded by the company as pre-tax income or expense.

wc.text: The increase in debt balances from December 31, 2025 was primarily due to capital structure activities required to effect the Vylor Separation, as well as higher short-term debt to fund the company’s working capital needs, including the Bayer resolution payment and the FMC rimisoxafen prepayment, as well as capital spending, dividend payments and share repurchases. In addition, long-term debt balances increased from December 31, 2025 due to the issuance of the Vylor 2031 Notes, the Vylor 2036 Notes and the Corteva 2036 Notes. See further information in Note 11 - Short-Term Borrowings, Long-Term Debt and Available Credit Facilities, to the interim Consolidated Financial Statements.

capex.text: The increase in debt balances from December 31, 2025 was primarily due to capital structure activities required to effect the Vylor Separation, as well as higher short-term debt to fund the company’s working capital needs, including the Bayer resolution payment and the FMC rimisoxafen prepayment, as well as capital spending, dividend payments and share repurchases. In addition, long-term debt balances increased from December 31, 2025 due to the issuance of the Vylor 2031 Notes, the Vylor 2036 Notes and the Corteva 2036 Notes. See further information in Note 11 - Short-Term Borrowings, Long-Term Debt and Available Credit Facilities, to the interim Consolidated Financial Statements.

fcf.text: The company also uses Free Cash Flow as a non-GAAP measure to evaluate and discuss its liquidity position and ability to generate cash. Free Cash Flow is defined as cash provided by (used for) operating activities – continuing operations, less capital expenditures. Management believes that Free Cash Flow provides investors with meaningful information regarding the company’s ongoing ability to generate cash through core operations, and the company’s ability to service its indebtedness, pay dividends (when declared), make share repurchases, and meet its ongoing cash needs for its operations.

net sales.heading: Net Sales
net sales.text: Net sales were $2,458 million and $2,618 million for the three months ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, respectively. The decrease was primarily driven by a 6 percent decrease in volume and a 2 percent decrease in price, partially offset by a 2 percent favorable impact from currency. The decrease in volume was driven by declines in both Seed and Crop Protection. Seed experienced volume declines across all regions due to timing shifts in North America, dry weather in EMEA and Asia Pacific, and the shift to soybean out-licensing in Latin America. Crop Protection volumes reflected weak market conditions in Brazil, partially offset by new product growth across all regions. The decrease in price was driven by competitive Crop Protection pricing in Latin America and North America acetochlor , partially offset by Seed pricing increases across all regions which were driven by higher out-licensing income and demand for top technology. The favorable currency impacts were driven by the Brazilian Real and South African Rand, partially offset by the Indian Rupee.
